title: Rate Limiting and Security Hardening
description: Implement rate limiting for authentication endpoints and apply security hardening techniques including security headers and anomaly detection.

data.text: **Rate limiting** restricts how many requests a client can make in a given time window. For authentication endpoints, rate limiting is critical because it slows down brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and denial-of-service attempts.

items: **Brute force**: Attackers try every possible password combination
**Credential stuffing**: Automated replay of leaked username/password pairs
**Password spraying**: Try a few common passwords against many accounts
**DoS**: Flood login endpoint to exhaust resources or lock accounts

data.title: Account Lockout vs Rate Limiting
data.text: Account lockout after 5 failed attempts is a denial-of-service vector. Attackers can lock out legitimate users. Rate limiting with exponential backoff is more user-friendly and harder to exploit.

The **token bucket** algorithm is the most common. It allows bursts of traffic up to a bucket size, then refills at a steady rate. For login endpoints, a token bucket with a small burst size and slow refill prevents brute force without blocking legitimate retries.

data.text: ASP.NET Core provides middleware for rate limiting. You can configure fixed-window or token-bucket policies. For auth endpoints, apply stricter limits than general API endpoints.

data.text: Rate limiting catches volume-based attacks but not sophisticated ones. **Anomaly detection** monitors behavioral patterns to spot suspicious activity that falls within rate limits.

items: **Impossible travel**: Login from two locations too far apart in time
**New device**: First login from an unrecognized device
**Time-of-day anomalies**: Account accessed at unusual hours
**IP reputation**: Requests from known malicious IPs

data.title: Progressive Friction
data.text: Instead of hard-blocking anomalies, apply progressive friction: step-up MFA, CAPTCHA, or email verification. Hard blocks frustrate legitimate users on new devices.
HTTP security headers instruct browsers to enforce security policies. They are simple to deploy and provide broad protection against common attacks.

For public endpoints like login and registration, CAPTCHAs add friction for bots while remaining invisible to most users. hCaptcha and reCAPTCHA v3 score users based on behavior and only challenge suspicious ones.

data.title: reCAPTCHA Verification

data.text: For admin portals, restrict access to known IP ranges using firewalls, API gateways, or application-level checks. Geo-blocking can prevent access from sanctioned countries but should not be the sole security control.

items.text: Apply rate limiting to all authentication endpoints
items.hint: Stricter limits for login than general API

items.text: Implement anomaly detection for login patterns
items.hint: New device, impossible travel, unusual hours
Use a library like NWebsec to avoid mistakes

items.text: Add CAPTCHA after repeated failed login attempts
items.hint: Progressive friction is better than immediate block

items.text: Log all authentication events with IP and user agent

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Rate limiting slows brute-force and credential stuffing
Anomaly detection catches sophisticated attacks within rate limits
Security headers provide broad browser-side protection
CAPTCHAs add friction for bots without annoying users
data.takeaway: Security hardening is a layered approach. No single control prevents all attacks.
